thesis: Wrongful destruction of evidence can leave an institution owing proportionate assistance against a later misdescription, even after fair compensation and accurate initial communication. The strongest version depends on a continuing protected use of the evidence, an actual additional obstacle caused by its loss, and assistance that preserves the distinction between historical findings, remedial entitlements, and procedural authority.
claimed_contribution: Section 2, “The contribution and its antecedents,” claims a “particular combination” rather than a new general theory: an established evidential breach, an authoritative practical decision, and an allegation that the decision does not determine. Section 3 supplies contrasting cases intended to identify when the breach grounds further assistance against another institution’s error.

findings.manuscript_location: Section 3, “From accurate records to substitute support”: “the original reason for repair can remain”; “a presumptive duty to provide a proportionate substitute.”
findings.claim: The general bridge to substitute performance has a close, uncited foundation in the continuity account of corrective justice.
findings.analysis: Gardner explains secondary duties through the surviving reasons for an unperformed primary obligation. His discussion also connects the appropriate substitute and recoverable consequences to the original obligation’s purpose. This closely matches the manuscript’s bridge and its restriction to protected uses. The omission concerns intellectual positioning; it does not demonstrate that the specific application was previously made. See [Gardner, author eprint, pp. 40, 46–50](https://johngardnerathome.info/pdfs/corrective.pdf).
findings.effect_on_conclusion: The general reparative principle cannot carry the novelty claim. The manuscript already describes itself as an application, so its principal conclusion need not fail.
findings.repair_conditions: Acknowledge this foundation and identify the additional work performed by the later-error case and its communication constraints.

findings.manuscript_location: Section 3, “From accurate records to substitute support”: “Funding the additional reasonable work can replace protection once supplied by the photographs.”
findings.claim: The extent of application-level novelty remains unresolved against established remedies for the cost of replacing lost evidential resources.
findings.analysis: Thompson expressly identifies expert and discovery costs for alternative proof as possible damages, although its holding concerns permission to proceed with a claim. Rule 37’s notes likewise discuss proportional replacement efforts and expense allocation. These are substantive antecedents to funded substitution, not merely similar terminology. Neither inspected text establishes the manuscript’s later administrative-misdescription case. See [Thompson, §III and note 7](https://caselaw.findlaw.com/court/in-court-of-appeals/1375916.html) and [Rule 37, 2015 Committee Note](https://www.law.cornell.edu/rules/frcp/rule_37).
findings.effect_on_conclusion: The assistance mechanism itself is established. What may remain distinctive is its application after closure, against an independently introduced error, while preserving a non-finding about the original allegation.
findings.repair_conditions: Compare that extension explicitly with existing substitution-cost remedies. Establishing a useful new application would suffice for the manuscript’s stated ambition; a new general obligation is unnecessary.

surviving_contribution: The inspected sources do not establish the complete combination developed in Sections 3–5. Its distinctive remainder is the comparison between two identical later errors: assistance has an additional reparative ground only where preservation would have supplied a usable, cheaper defence. The lost material can answer the narrower accusation of invented damage without proving contractor responsibility. This is joined to constraints on assistance: preserve the entitlement and any legitimate procedural effect, authenticate the institution’s non-finding, and leave independent testimony assessable. This remains a potentially distinct worked application and synthesis, not an established claim of priority.
remaining_questions: Section 3 says that “a genuine lost opportunity can justify assistance without certainty of victory.” How should the existing evidential-damage literature determine the required showing of relevance and the extent of assistance when the photographs’ contents are uncertain?

Section 6 ends the residual duty when “an adequate substitute is in place.” What distinguishes discharge of a reasonable assistance duty from successful epistemic repair, especially when an audience continues to reject an accurate correction?
Could the inaccessible portions of Porat and Stein or Friedman already encompass these later expenses under their broader remedial accounts? Their accessible passages cannot settle that comparison.
limitations: The complete supplied manuscript, including its bibliography, was read. Its supplied hash was used only as an identifier and was not recomputed.
Research used public web search and public source openings only. No manuscript identity, project history, other manuscript, private material, or author contact was sought.
This was a finite English-language search as of 31 October 2026. No manuscript completion date was supplied, so publication chronology does not establish priority over the manuscript’s composition.

Porat and Stein’s repository abstract and Friedman’s repository introductory passage were accessible, but their linked full texts returned HTTP 403. Their narrow cited attributions are supported; their complete arguments and possible closer overlaps remain unchecked.
Full source availability does not mean every page was read. The source inventory identifies the passages actually inspected.

Hull’s publisher page provided an abstract and notes, not the full argument. Attempts to retrieve Lackey’s 2022 address through PhilArchive and the APA failed; JSTOR returned no usable text. Neither was treated as a fully read predecessor.

Matsunaga’s article on reparations bureaucracy and Lisle-Mainwaring on continuing reputational mitigation appeared as relevant search leads, but their opened pages were blocked. Their snippets were not used to establish findings.
The legal materials were used as historical and conceptual comparators. A comprehensive check of their current precedential treatment, or of every jurisdiction’s law, was not undertaken.

closest_predecessors.difference: His inspected discussion addresses adjudicative roles and sanctions, rather than support against a later administrative misdescription.
closest_predecessors.remaining_contribution: The continuing assistance duty and the two-variant causal comparison remain beyond this discussion.

closest_predecessors.overlap: Gardner supplies the general rationale for substitute performance serving an original duty’s purpose.

closest_predecessors.overlap: Flowerree explains why an offered communication can fail as repair because of audience reception.
closest_predecessors.difference: Her account concerns successful knowledge-producing repair; the manuscript’s duty supports a fair opportunity without guaranteeing belief.
closest_predecessors.remaining_contribution: A bounded assistance duty grounded in the custodian’s particular impairment remains distinct.

closest_predecessors.overlap: Altanian makes victims’ standing as epistemic contributors part of repair.
closest_predecessors.difference: Her argument concerns genocide, denialism, and unjust epistemic practices, rather than a limited preservation undertaking.

closest_predecessors.evidence_location: Manuscript §4, “Helping her speak in her own right”; Altanian §4, paragraphs on epistemic contribution and relational equality.

closest_predecessors.remaining_contribution: The manuscript isolates a continuing capacity-based obligation rather than a general theory of epistemic remainders.
closest_predecessors.evidence_location: Manuscript §3, “Payment for the first loss does not necessarily restore the second”; Lambrecht §§3 and 6–7.

citation_audit.evidence: Identity, year, journal, and starting page match. The [repository abstract](https://larc.cardozo.yu.edu/clr/vol18/iss6/3/) expressly supports both attributed remedies. The manuscript accurately identifies its cited evidence as an abstract. The linked full article was inaccessible, preventing a complete scope comparison.

citation_audit.evidence: The [author-hosted PDF](https://nissenbaum.tech.cornell.edu/papers/Contextual%20Integrity%20Up%20and%20Down.pdf) confirms the reference. Pages 225–226 explain appropriate contextual flows; pp. 255–256 address transformed data, transparency, and accountability. This supports the limited attribution, without independently establishing the manuscript’s reparative debt.

citation_audit.manuscript_location: Section 5, “Binding a question without proving its answer”: convictions should “support rational belief in guilt” and provide grounds for ending ordinary inquiry.
citation_audit.evidence: The [published LSE copy](https://eprints.lse.ac.uk/120199/1/Criminal_proof.pdf) confirms the citation. Section IV, especially pp. 1086–1087, supports both claims. The manuscript appropriately restricts this account to criminal conviction rather than all institutional outcomes.

citation_audit.manuscript_location: Section 5, “Binding a question without proving its answer”: “defeasible institutional testimony.”
